claim: Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) affects about 1–3% of women under 40 years of age.
source: Primary ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a major cause of female infertility and affects about 1–3% of women under 40 years of age.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact presented in the introduction without specific citation, drawing from established scientific knowledge about POI prevalence.

claim: POI is characterized by cessation of ovarian function before the age of 40 years.
source: It is characterized by cessation of ovarian function before the age of 40 years.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about POI that represents established medical knowledge.

claim: Genetic causes of POI account for approximately 20% of cases.
source: Genetic causes of POI account for approximately 20% of cases (Rossetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rossetti et al., 2017.

claim: The S167L missense variant in HSF2BP was identified in a consanguineous family with three cases of POI.
source: Using whole-exome sequencing in a family with three cases of POI, we identified the candidate missense variant S167L in HSF2BP, an essential meiotic gene.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by whole-exome sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The HSF2BP-S167L variant behaves as a hypomorphic allele compared to a loss-of-function mouse model.
source: Functional analysis of the HSF2BP-S167L variant in mouse showed that it behaves as a hypomorphic allele compared to a new loss-of-function (knock-out) mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative functional analysis data from mouse models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L females show reduced fertility with smaller litter sizes.
source: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L females show reduced fertility with smaller litter sizes.
evidence: This is supported by fertility assessment data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: C19ORF57/BRME1 was identified as a strong interactor and stabilizer of HSF2BP.
source: To obtain mechanistic insights, we identified C19ORF57/BRME1 as a strong interactor and stabilizer of HSF2BP
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid screening, co-immunoprecipitation, and protein stability data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The BRME1/HSF2BP protein complex co-immunoprecipitates with BRCA2, RAD51, RPA and PALB2.
source: showed that the BRME1/HSF2BP protein complex co-immunoprecipitates with BRCA2, RAD51, RPA and PALB2.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Meiocytes bearing the HSF2BP-S167L variant showed a strongly decreased staining of both HSF2BP and BRME1 at the recombination nodules.
source: Meiocytes bearing the HSF2BP-S167L variant showed a strongly decreased staining of both HSF2BP and BRME1 at the recombination nodules
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: Meiocytes bearing the HSF2BP-S167L variant showed a reduced number of the foci formed by the recombinases RAD51/DMC1.
source: and a reduced number of the foci formed by the recombinases RAD51/DMC1, thus leading to a lower frequency of crossovers.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The HSF2BP-S167L variant leads to a lower frequency of crossovers.
source: and a reduced number of the foci formed by the recombinases RAD51/DMC1, thus leading to a lower frequency of crossovers.
evidence: This is supported by MLH1 and CDK2 foci quantification data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The variant rs200655253 (21:43630396 G > A, GRCh38) in HSF2BP changes a TCG codon into a TTG (NP_008962.1:p.Ser167Leu).
source: The variant lies within the sixth exon of the reference transcript ENST00000291560.7 (NM_007031.2:c.500C > T) and changes a TCG codon into a TTG (NP_008962.1:p.Ser167Leu).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic variant identified through whole exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

claim: The S167L variant has a Variant Allele Frequency of 0.0001845 in the GnomAD database.
source: It is very rare (Variant Allele Frequency/VAF 0.0001845 in the GnomAD database and 0.0005 in the GME Variome dedicated to Middle-East populations)
evidence: This is data from public genomic databases.

claim: The S167L variant is absent in a homozygous state from all available databases.
source: and absent in a homozygous state from all available databases.
evidence: This is information from database queries.

claim: Serine 167 is a highly conserved position.
source: Serine 167 is a highly conserved position
evidence: This is supported by multiple sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The S167L variant is predicted to be pathogenic or deleterious by 11 out of the 18 pathogenicity predictors available in dbNSFP 3.5.
source: and the S167L variant is predicted to be pathogenic or deleterious by 11 out of the 18 pathogenicity predictors available in dbNSFP 3.5.
evidence: This is based on computational prediction tools applied to the variant.

claim: The variant segregates in a Mendelian fashion within the family.
source: The variant was verified by Sanger sequencing and was found to segregate in a Mendelian fashion within the family
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All affected family members are homozygous for the HSF2BP-S167L variant.
source: the affected twin III-1 was homozygous for the variant and both parents and fertile siblings were heterozygous carriers
evidence: This is supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: HSF2BP is essential for meiotic recombination through its ability to interact with BRCA2.
source: During the course of this work and, in agreement with our results, two independent groups showed that HSF2BP is essential for meiotic recombination through its ability to interact with BRCA2 (Brandsma et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to two independent studies.

claim: Genetic disruption of Hsf2bp in mouse leads to the accumulation of γH2AX and RPA on chromosome axes.
source: Both groups showed that genetic disruption of Hsf2bp in mouse leads to the accumulation in the chromosomes axes of DNA repair proteins such as γH2AX (ATR-dependent phosphorylation of H2AX marks DSBs) and the single stranded-DNA binding protein RPA
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brandsma et al., 2019 and Zhang et al., 2019, and confirmed by data in Figure 4.

claim: Genetic disruption of Hsf2bp in mouse leads to a strong reduction of the recombinases DMC1 and RAD51 at the recombination nodules.
source: a strong reduction of the recombinases DMC1 and RAD51 at the RNs
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data in Figure 5.

claim: Genetic disruption of Hsf2bp in mouse leads to a lack of crossovers as labelled by MLH1.
source: and a lack of COs as labelled by MLH1 (Baker et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data in Figure 6.

claim: Loss of HSF2BP in male mice results in sterility.
source: The end result is male sterility (Brandsma, 2006; Brandsma et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: Loss of HSF2BP in female mice showed a milder meiotic phenotype.
source: However, loss of HSF2BP in female mice showed a milder meiotic phenotype (Zhang et al., 2019 and our own data, see below)
evidence: This is supported by citation and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L male mice showed a slight non-significant reduction in fertility.
source: whilst males only showed a slight non-significant reduction in fertility (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is supported by fertility assessment data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Hsf2bp-/- ovaries showed a strong depletion of follicles.
source: Hsf2bp-/- ovaries but not Hsf2bp+/+ and Hsf2bpS167L/S167L showed a strong depletion of follicles.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L ovaries showed no apparent differences in the number of follicles compared to wild-type animals.
source: Histological analysis of Hsf2bpS167L/S167L ovaries revealed no apparent differences in the number of follicles in comparison to wild-type (WT) animals (Figure 2b–c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: Testes from Hsf2bpS167L/S167L mice displayed a 21% reduction in size compared to WT mice.
source: Testes from Hsf2bpS167L/S167L mice displayed a reduced size (21% reduction compared to WT mice; testis/body weight ratio: S167L 0.26% ± 0.07 (n = 12) vs 0.33% ± 0.05 for WT controls (n = 14), **p<0,01, Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: This is supported by testis weight measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Testes from Hsf2bp-/- mice displayed a 70% reduction in size compared to WT mice.
source: and this reduction was stronger in Hsf2bp-/- testes (70% reduction compared to WT, testis/body weight ratio: Hsf2bp-/- 0.10% ± 0.005 (n = 6) vs 0.33% ± 0.05 for WT controls (n = 14) ****p<0,001, Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by testis weight measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L testes revealed seminiferous tubules with a partial arrest with apoptotic spermatocytes.
source: Histological analysis of adult Hsf2bpS167L/S167L testes revealed seminiferous tubules with a partial arrest with apoptotic spermatocytes (meiotic divisions) and their epididymis exhibited scarcer spermatozoa (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L males showed increased numbers of meiotic divisions positive for TUNEL staining.
source: Consistent with these results, Hsf2bpS167L/S167L males showed increased numbers of meiotic divisions positive for TUNEL staining (Figure 2f)
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L males showed a reduction in the number of spermatozoa in the epididymis (3.3 × 10^6 vs 4.3 × 10^6 in WT).
source: and a reduction in the number of spermatozoa in the epididymis (3.3 × 106 in the Hsf2bpS167L/S167L mutant vs 4.3 × 106 in the WT; Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The seminiferous epithelium of Hsf2bp-/- mice showed a stage IV arrest.
source: Following these criteria, the seminiferous epithelium of Hsf2bp-/- mice showed a stage IV arrest, characterized by a massive apoptosis of zygotene-like spermatocytes occurring at the same time that In spermatogonia divide into B spermatogonia (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L meiocytes showed no difference in synapsis and desynapsis from leptotene to diplotene in both oocytes and spermatocytes.
source: We did not observe any difference in synapsis and desynapsis from leptotene to diplotene in both oocytes and spermatocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis of SYCP1 and SYCP3 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: Hsf2bp-/- spermatocytes were arrested at a zygotene-like stage.
source: As expected, this phenotype was exacerbated in Hsf2bp-/- spermatocytes that were arrested at a zygotene-like stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Hsf2bp-/- oocytes showed a delay in prophase I progression with the majority of cells at zygotene stage in 17.5 dpc females.
source: Hsf2bp-/- oocytes showed a delay in prophase I progression with the majority of cells at zygotene stage in 17.5 days post-coitum (dpc) females, whilst the WT oocytes were mainly at pachytene stage.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Hsf2bp-/- oocytes showed increased numbers of oocytes with synapsis defects (45.5% ± 1.5 vs 7.5% ± 1.5 in WT).
source: Additionally, we observed increased numbers of oocytes showing synapsis defects in the Hsf2bp-/- oocytes (Hsf2bp-/-: 45,5% ± 1,5 vs WT: 7,5% ± 1,5; n = 2 (both genotypes), **p<0,01, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis and quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L meiocytes showed a striking reduction of HSF2BP staining at the axes during prophase I in both spermatocytes and oocytes.
source: We observed a striking reduction of HSF2BP staining at the axes during prophase I in both spermatocytes and oocytes (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis and quantification shown in Figure 3a-b.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed that the reduced HSF2BP labeling in Hsf2bpS167L/S167L meiocytes correlated with a reduced protein expression level.
source: Western blot analysis of WT, Hsf2bpS167L/S167L and Hsf2bp-/- in whole testis extracts from 13 days post-partum (dpp) animals (Figure 3c) revealed that the reduced labeling observed by immunofluorescence correlated with a reduced protein expression level
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The S167L mutation leads to reduced expression and/or stability of HSF2BP.
source: suggesting that the mutation leads to a reduced expression and/or stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the western blot and immunofluorescence data showing reduced protein levels.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L spermatocytes showed an increased labeling of γH2AX at pachytene.
source: Our results revealed that Hsf2bpS167L/S167L spermatocytes showed an increased labeling of γH2AX at pachytene (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L spermatocytes showed an accumulation of RPA at the chromosome axis.
source: an accumulation of RPA at the chromosome axis (Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis and quantification shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L spermatocytes showed a reduction of the recombinases DMC1 and RAD51 staining.
source: a reduction of the recombinases DMC1 and RAD51 staining (Figure 5a–b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–b)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis and quantification shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L spermatocytes showed an accumulation of SPATA22.
source: an accumulation of SPATA22 (Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis and quantification shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L spermatocytes showed a decreased number of crossovers measured as MLH1.
source: and a decreased number of COs (measured as MLH1, Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis and quantification shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L mice showed the presence of univalents in the XY pair at pachynema.
source: In accordance with the reduction of COs, we observed the presence of univalents in the XY pair at pachynema as well as univalents in metaphase I spermatocytes from Hsf2bpS167L/S167L mice (Figure 6d and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Both HSF2BP-WT and HSF2BP-S167L co-immunoprecipitate with BRCA2-C similarly.
source: Our results showed that BRCA2-C co-immunoprecipitates with both HSF2BP-WT and HSF2BP-S167L in similar ways (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a.

claim: HSF2BP and BRCA2-C show a nuclear dotted pattern when co-transfected.
source: This pattern changed drastically to a nuclear dotted pattern when co-transfected (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The re-localization of HSF2BP and BRCA2-C to a nuclear dotted pattern was independent of the HSF2BP variant.
source: This re-localization was independent of the HSF2BP variant, suggesting that the HSF2BP variant effects are not directly mediated by BRCA2 delocalization.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing similar patterns for both WT and S167L variants.

claim: 19 out of 98 analyzed clones from yeast two-hybrid screening matched the uncharacterized gene 4930432K21Rik (C19ORF57/BRME1).
source: The analysis of the clones with putative interactors revealed that 19 out of 98 analyzed clones matched the uncharacterized gene 4930432K21Rik, which corresponds to human C19ORF57, hereby dubbed BRME1 for Break Repair Meiotic recombinase recruitment factor 1.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid screening data.

claim: BRME1 consists of 600 amino acids with a high content of acidic residues.
source: This HSF2BP interactor consists of 600 amino acids with a high content of acidic residues, has no recognizable functional domains and is intrinsically disordered.
evidence: This is a description of the protein characteristics based on sequence analysis.

claim: Both HSF2BP-S167L and WT interact with BRME1.
source: Both HSF2BP-S167L and WT interacted with BRME1 (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The HSF2BP/BRME1-interacting domain is mapped to the C-term fragment of BRME1 (spanning residues 475–600).
source: We mapped the HSF2BP/BRME1-interacting domain to the C-term fragment of BRME1 (spanning residues 475–600 of the murine protein, Figure 7c).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with BRME1 deletion constructs shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Brme1Δ142-472/Δ142-472 mutant mice were fertile and did not show defects in chromosome synapsis.
source: In line with this, the Brme1Δ142-472/Δ142-472 mutant mice, expressing the BRME1 protein devoid of its central part, were fertile and did not show defects in chromosome synapsis or an alteration of HSF2BP loading to axes
evidence: This is supported by fertility assessment and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: BRME1 localizes to the chromosome axes of WT meiocytes from zygotene to pachytene with a pattern of discrete foci that mimics the recombination nodules.
source: BRME1 localized to the chromosome axes of WT meiocytes from zygotene to pachytene with a pattern of discrete foci that mimics the RNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: BRME1 perfectly co-localized with HSF2BP on the chromosome axes.
source: In agreement with the yeast two hybrid and co-IP results, BRME1 perfectly co-localized with HSF2BP on the chromosome axes (Figure 7d and Supplementary file 1d for quantification).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 7d-e.

claim: HSF2BP and BRME1 showed higher levels of spatio-temporal colocalization at the recombination nodules with RPA than with DMC1.
source: During prophase I, HSF2BP and BRME1 showed higher levels of spatio-temporal colocalization at the RNs with RPA than with DMC1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 3a–b and Supplementary files 1d-e for quantification).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hsf2bp-/- meiocytes showed a complete lack of BRME1 staining.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of meiocytes showed a complete lack of BRME1 staining in the absence of HSF2BP
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7f-g.

claim: Hsf2bpS167L/S167L meiocytes showed a significant reduction of BRME1 foci number (35% reduction in males and 72% in females at pachytene).
source: and a significant reduction of foci number in the presence of HSF2BP-S167L variant (35% reduction in males and 72% in females at pachytene; Figure 7f–g and Figure 7—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 7f-g.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed a drastic reduction of BRME1 expression in Hsf2bpS167L/S167L and Hsf2bp-/- spermatocytes.
source: Western blot analysis also revealed a drastic reduction of BRME1 expression in Hsf2bpS167L/S167L and Hsf2bp-/- spermatocytes, suggesting an HSF2BP-dependent stabilization of BRME1 (Figure 7h).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7h.

claim: Both HSF2BP and BRME1 lacked direct DNA-binding abilities.
source: Our results show that both proteins lacked direct DNA-binding abilities, in contrast to the strong activity of RPA (Figure 7—figure supplement 4b–c).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro DNA binding assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4b-c.

claim: None of the recombination-deficient mutants abrogate BRME1 labeling at zygotene, in contrast to its absence of loading in SPO11-deficient mice.
source: We were able to show that none of the recombination-deficient mutants abrogate BRME1 labeling at zygotene (or the corresponding meiotic stage at which the mutant spermatocytes are arrested), in contrast to its absence of loading in SPO11-deficient mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 6b, left).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in various mutant backgrounds shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 6b.

claim: SPO11-dependent DSBs are essential for targeting HSF2BP/BRME1 to the recombination nodules.
source: These results are very similar to those obtained for HSF2BP in these mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 6b, right) and indicate that SPO11-dependent DSBs are essential for targeting HSF2BP/BRME1 to the RNs
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data showing absence of HSF2BP/BRME1 only in SPO11-deficient mice.

claim: Brme1-/- females showed a strong reduction of the follicle pool.
source: Brme1-/- females, despite being fertile, showed a strong reduction of the follicle pool (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Brme1-/- males were infertile.
source: Male Brme1-/- mice were infertile
evidence: This is supported by fertility assessment and histological analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Brme1-/- males showed a 76% reduction in testis size compared to WT.
source: the average size of their testes was severely reduced (76% reduction compared to WT; testis weight/body weight ratio: Brme1-/- 0,08% ± 0004 (n = 6) vs 0,33% ± 0,05 for WT controls (n = 14), ****p<0.0001, Figure 8b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: This is supported by testis weight measurements shown in Figure 8b.

claim: Brme1-/- males lacked spermatozoa.
source: and lacked spermatozoa (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Brme1-/- spermatocytes were partially synapsed and showed a partner-switch phenotype.
source: Double immunolabeling of SYCP3 and SYCP1 revealed that spermatocytes were partially synapsed and showed a partner-switch phenotype in which synapsis is not restricted to homologous pairs (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Brme1-/- spermatocytes arrest at a zygotene-like stage with a small fraction of cells (3.7% ± 1.9) able to escape to early pachytene.
source: The arrest corresponds to a zygotene-like stage though a small fraction of cells (3,7% ± 1,9; n = 3) were able to escape this blockage reaching early pachytene.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Brme1-/- oocytes showed an increased number of cells with different degree of asynapsis (47.9% ± 2.2 vs 12% ± 5.7 in WT).
source: Brme1-/- oocyte spread analysis revealed the presence of a subset of fully synapsed pachynemas but an increased number of cells with different degree of asynapsis (47,9% ± 2,2 vs 12% ± 5,7 in the WT; n = 2 (both genotypes), *p<0,05 Figure 8e and Figure 8—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 8e.

claim: Brme1-/- spermatocytes showed a strong reduction of HSF2BP staining.
source: Our results showed a strong reduction of HSF2BP staining in BRME1-null spermatocytes (Figure 8f)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8f.

claim: Brme1-/- oocytes showed a total absence of HSF2BP staining.
source: and a total absence in oocytes (Figure 8g).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8g.

claim: Western blot analysis showed a strong reduction of HSF2BP in 13 dpp testis extracts from Brme1-/- mice.
source: Western blot analysis of HSF2BP in 13 dpp testis extracts from Brme1-/- mice showed a strong reduction in comparison with the WT control (Figure 8h)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8h.

claim: Brme1-/- spermatocytes showed an accumulation of γH2AX and RPA on zygonema-like spermatocytes.
source: Immunostaining of Brme1-/- spermatocytes for γH2AX, RPA, the recombinases RAD51 and DMC1 or SPATA22 revealed an accumulation of γH2AX and RPA on zygonema-like spermatocytes (Figure 9—figure supplement 1a–b)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: Brme1-/- spermatocytes showed a drastic reduction of RAD51/DMC1 foci in early and late zygonema.
source: a drastic reduction of RAD51/DMC1 foci in early and late zygonema (Figure 9a and c, Figure 9—figure supplement 2a and c)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 9a and c.

claim: Brme1-/- spermatocytes showed a strong accumulation of SPATA22.
source: and a strong accumulation of SPATA22 (Figure 9e and Figure 9—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 9e.

claim: Brme1-/- spermatocytes showed a total absence of crossovers as measured by MLH1 staining.
source: According to the meiotic arrest at the zygotene-like stage, MLH1 staining revealed a total absence of COs (Figure 9g).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9g.

claim: Brme1-/- oocytes showed an accumulation of γH2AX.
source: As in males, Brme1-/- oocytes showed an accumulation of γH2AX (Figure 9—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Brme1-/- oocytes showed an accumulation of SPATA22.
source: and SPATA22 (Figure 9f and Figure 9—figure supplement 2f)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9f.

claim: Brme1-/- oocytes showed a reduced staining of DMC1 and RAD51 leading to a reduced number of crossovers.
source: and a reduced staining of DMC1 and RAD51 leading to a reduced number of COs (measured as interstitial CDK2; Figure 9b, d and h, Figure 9—figure supplement 2b and d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 9b, d, and h.

claim: Brme1-/- oocytes did not show RPA accumulation.
source: However, Brme1-/- oocytes did not show RPA accumulation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1d.

claim: BRME1 immunoprecipitates from testis extracts identified HSF2BP as the main interactor, but also BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51 and RPA.
source: We identified as expected HSF2BP as the main interactor, but also BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51 and RPA, strongly suggesting that they form a large multimeric complex (Supplementary files 1g-1h).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation coupled to mass spectrometry data.

claim: BRME1 co-immunoprecipitated with BRCA2 and HSF2BP when they were all co-transfected.
source: BRME1 co-immunoprecipitated with BRCA2 and HSF2BP when they were all co-transfected, but importantly BRME1 alone did not co-immunoprecitate with BRCA2 (Figure 10a–b).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10a-b.

claim: HSF2BP showed modest but positive co-IP with RPA, PALB2 and RAD51.
source: We also observed modest but positive co-IP of HSF2BP with RPA, PALB2 and RAD51
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1a.

claim: BRME1 showed modest but positive co-IP with RAD51 and RPA but not with PALB2.
source: and of BRME1 with RAD51 and RPA but not with PALB2 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1a.

claim: In a cell-free TNT system, there was an absence of direct interaction between HSF2BP/BRME1 and other proteins, with the exception of BRME1 and HSF2BP.
source: We observed an absence of direct interaction between any of them, with the exception of BRME1 and HSF2BP, as expected from the Y2H analysis (Figure 10—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by TNT co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1b.

claim: When HSF2BP was co-overexpressed with BRME1, its pattern changed to an intense nucleoplasm staining with nuclear invaginations that resemble nucleoplasmic reticulum.
source: However, when HSF2BP was co-overexpressed with BRME1, its pattern changed to an intense nucleoplasm staining with nuclear invaginations that resemble nucleoplasmic reticulum (Figure 10c; Malhas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10c.

claim: Nuclear invaginations were reduced when BRME1 was co-transfected with HSF2BP-S167L.
source: Interestingly, such invaginations were reduced when BRME1 was co-transfected with HSF2BP-S167L (Figure 10c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 10c.

claim: The intensity of the fluorescence signal of HSF2BP-S167L was lower than for HSF2BP-WT.
source: In addition, the intensity of the fluorescence signal of HSF2BP-S167L was lower than for HSF2BP-WT and both intensities increased when HSF2BP was co-expressed with BRME1 (Figure 10c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10c.

claim: Western blot analysis indicated a reduced protein stability of the S167L variant.
source: Western blot analysis indicated a reduced protein stability of the S167L variant (Figure 10d)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 10d.

claim: The protein expression level of transfected HSF2BP increased when co-transfected with BRME1.
source: Interestingly, the protein expression level of transfected HSF2BP increased when co-transfected with BRME1 and was partially dependent on proteasome degradation (Figure 10d)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data with and without proteasome inhibitor shown in Figure 10d.

claim: The causality of the HSF2BP-S167L variant is supported by the meiotic phenotype and the subfertility observed in Hsf2bpS167L/S167L female mice.
source: The causality of the HSF2BP-S167L variant is supported by the meiotic phenotype and the subfertility observed in Hsf2bpS167L/S167L female mice.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the combined data from mouse models.

claim: The DNA repair defects in murine Hsf2bpS167L/S167L meiocytes provide evidence that this missense variant alters meiotic recombination.
source: Furthermore, the DNA repair defects in murine Hsf2bpS167L/S167L meiocytes, displayed by the reduced number of RAD51/DMC1 foci on DSBs and the subsequent reduction in the number of COs, provide evidence that this missense variant alters meiotic recombination.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the immunofluorescence data.

claim: The comparative analysis of the S167L allele with the Hsf2bp null allele revealed that the missense variant can be considered as a hypomorphic allele.
source: This conclusion was further supported by the comparative analysis of the S167L allele with the Hsf2bp null allele, which revealed that the missense variant can be considered as a hypomorphic allele.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on comparative phenotypic analysis.

claim: The identification of HSF2BP as a gene implicated in POI is in line with recent reports of POI-causing variants in genes required for DNA repair and recombination.
source: Our identification of HSF2BP as a gene implicated in POI is in line with recent reports of POI-causing variants in genes that are required for DNA repair and recombination, such as MCM8, MCM9, SYCE1, MSH4, PSMC3IP, FANCM or NBN (AlAsiri et al., 2015; Carlosama et al., 2017; de Vries et al., 2014; Fouquet et al., 2017; He et al., 2018; Tenenbaum-Rakover et al., 2015; Tucker et al., 2018; Wood-Trageser et al., 2014; Zangen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a contextual statement supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Meiotic mouse mutants often exhibit sexually dimorphic phenotypes.
source: Meiotic mouse mutants often exhibit sexually dimorphic phenotypes (Cahoon and Libuda, 2019).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by a citation.

claim: The organization of the axial elements is known to be different between sexes.
source: These differences can have a structural basis, given that the organization of the axial elements is known to be different between sexes.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: The meiotic cohesin subunit RAD21L plays an essential role in males but not in females.
source: This is supported by the difference in length of the axes and by the essential role that the meiotic cohesin subunit RAD21L plays in males but not in females (Herrán et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Herrán et al., 2011.

claim: In general, meiotic recombination mutants appear to proceed further in female than in male.
source: In general, meiotic recombination mutants appear to proceed further in female than in male, because in males the asynapsis of the sex bivalent leads to a loss of silencing of the Y chromosome, and perhaps also because of the presence of less stringent checkpoints in oogenesis (Hunt and Hassold, 2002).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by a citation.

claim: A strong reduction of the spermatozoa count (up to 60%) does not affect male mouse fertility.
source: However, it is known that a strong reduction of the spermatozoa count (up to 60%) does not affect male mouse fertility (Schürmann et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schürmann et al., 2002.

claim: The sub-fertility observed in HSF2BP-S167L female mice appears to be milder in comparison to the phenotype of the human patients.
source: Although we cannot exclude that a POI-like phenotype would appear over time in HSF2BP-S167L female mice, the sub-fertility observed in HSF2BP-S167L females appears to be milder in comparison to the phenotype of the human patients.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement comparing mouse and human phenotypes.

claim: Mice may have lower sensitivity to hypomorphic alleles compared to humans.
source: This could be explained by a lower sensitivity of mice to hypomorphic alleles compared to humans, in a similar manner to the known lower gene dosage sensitivity of the former in the context of genes that are haploinsufficient in human (Veitia, 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: The initial events of human female meiosis appear to be more error-prone than in mice.
source: In addition, the initial events of human female meiosis appear to be more error-prone than in mice, or even than human males, as evidenced by the increased incidence of synaptic defects in the human oocytes or the fact that MLH1 foci appear much earlier in prophase I (Hassold et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hassold et al., 2007.

claim: Human oocytes exhibit a specific crossover maturation inefficiency.
source: Furthermore, it has recently been shown that human oocytes exhibit a specific CO maturation inefficiency (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Despite a higher total number of crossovers in women, the frequency of bivalents without crossover is paradoxically higher in women than in men.
source: Indeed, despite a higher total number of COs in women, the frequency of bivalents without CO is paradoxically higher in women than in men.
evidence: This is a statement about human meiosis supported by the context of the Wang et al., 2017 citation.

claim: Another variant of HSF2BP (G224*) was shown to affect recombination rate in males.
source: Although future studies might identify infertile men homozygous for the S167L variant, it is interesting to note that another variant of HSF2BP (G224*) was shown to affect recombination rate in males and that two siblings homozygous for this HSF2BP variant in the analyzed Icelandic population were healthy but without descendants, suggesting they were infertile (Halldorsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Halldorsson et al., 2019.

claim: BRCA2 is a multidomain hub protein.
source: These interactions could possibly be mediated by the multidomain hub protein BRCA2 (Siaud et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siaud et al., 2011.

claim: BRCA2 directly interacts with the DSBs recruiter PALB2, with the recombinases RAD51 and DMC1, and with DNA.
source: In addition, BRCA2 also directly interacts with the DSBs recruiter PALB2, with the recombinases RAD51 and DMC1 (through different specific domains), and with DNA (Siaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siaud et al., 2011.

claim: Genes with recently identified variants in POI patients are implicated in the repair of induced DSBs at the early stages of meiosis and encode BRCA2-interacting factors.
source: Interestingly, genes with recently identified variants in POI patients are implicated in the repair of induced DSBs at the early stages of meiosis and encode BRCA2-interacting factors, such as MEIOB, DMC1 or BRCA2 itself (Caburet et al., 2019a; Caburet et al., 2020; Caburet et al., 2019b; He et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: HSF2BP is one of the very few human genes with variants known to affect both the genome-wide recombination rate in the human population and meiotic chromosome missegregation (fertility).
source: To our knowledge, HSF2BP is one of the very few human genes with variants known to affect both the genome-wide recombination rate in the human population and meiotic chromosome missegregation (fertility) through a reduction of the recombination rate (Halldorsson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Halldorsson et al., 2019.

claim: Variants in genes involved in meiotic recombination and SC constituents could be responsible for a large fraction of genetic infertilities.
source: Specifically, variants in genes involved in meiotic recombination and SC constituents could be responsible for a large fraction of genetic infertilities.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings and context.

claim: Variants with sexual phenotypic dimorphism are not under strong purifying selection because individuals of one sex are fertile carriers.
source: However, this is not the case for genes with sexual phenotypic dimorphism (Gershoni and Pietrokovski, 2014) as is apparent for a wide number of meiotic genes (Cahoon and Libuda, 2019), including HSF2BP and BRME1, where individuals of one of the sexes are fertile carriers.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement supported by citations.
